Portugal's median square metre: €2,264. Up 17.7% in a year.

That's INE's figure for homes sold in the 12 months to June 2026, released on October 23. A year earlier it was €1,923.

We read it as space, because that's how people abroad ask the question. At the median, €300,000 buys more than 100 m² in 281 of the 304 municipalities with an INE figure. In Lisbon, about 58 m². In Porto, 83. In Grândola, Comporta's municipality, 118.

The document puts it on nine pages: the national line since 2016 (+173%), what €500,000 buys in six places, what a non-resident pays to close, and the gross yield INE's rent data gives (5.2% nationally, before costs and tax).

Medians aren't homes. They're the middle of everything sold in a year, new and existing, and they don't describe prime areas inside a municipality. They show where a budget goes further.

From December 1, the same figures sit on one map, for readers in Luxembourg, France, Switzerland, Brazil, the US and Israel.

$500,000 in Portugal, five places.

At the ECB rate of October 23 ($1.1193 to the euro), $500,000 is €446,708. Divided by INE's median price per m² of homes sold in the year to June 2026, it buys 86 m² in Lisbon, 91 in Cascais, 108 in Loulé in the Algarve, 123 in Porto and 176 in Grândola, Comporta's municipality.

US clients meet two sets of rules before they meet a floor plan.

On the Portuguese side, a non-resident pays IMT at a flat 7.5% on a home, unless an exception applies, such as becoming a Portuguese tax resident within two years.

On the US side, money waiting in a Portuguese bank account counts toward the $10,000 FBAR threshold. If they later live in Portugal, the Form 8938 thresholds for taxpayers abroad are $200,000 at year end or $300,000 at any time ($400,000 and $600,000 for joint filers).

We describe the rules and the numbers; advice on a client's case stays with their lawyer and tax adviser. The map, in dollars, is in the first comment.
